Hatchlings of the cockatoo squid emerge from their egg capsules at a remarkably small size, with a mantle length at birth of only 1.3 cm [Lb = 1.3 cm]. This diminutive neonate stage is followed by a sustained period of somatic growth that spans several years in the cold, deep waters of the North Pacific. The species exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in size, with females attaining considerably larger dimensions than males over their lifespan. Field records indicate that female cockatoo squid approach a mantle length at death of 270 cm [Li = 270 cm], a figure that places them among the most elongate of the cranchiid squids. This extreme size is accompanied by a correspondingly large mass; based on size-corrected allometric relationships from related ommastrephids, the wet weight at death for a female of this mantle length is estimated at approximately 198,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 198,000 grams]. The ecological implications of such a large body plan are substantial, influencing everything from buoyancy regulation via ammonium chloride reservoirs to the spectrum of prey items that become available to the adult squid.

Reproductive investment in this species is characterized by a modest allocation of somatic tissue to gamete production when considered against its immense body size. At the ambient temperatures typical of its mesopelagic habitat, measured at 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) is estimated to be around 15% [GSI = around 15%]. This value suggests that a relatively small fraction of the female's total body mass is devoted to reproductive tissue at any given time, a pattern that may reflect the energetic constraints of a cold, low-productivity environment. The onset of reproductive capability is not immediate; females undergo a prolonged period of maturation before they are physiologically prepared for spawning. The mantle length at puberty for females has been recorded at 100 cm [Lp = 100 cm], a size that signals the activation of gonadal development and the beginning of a shift in energy allocation from purely somatic growth toward reproductive preparation.

Under the cold thermal conditions of its native habitat, consistently at 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the total lifespan for a female is estimated to be approximately three years, or about 1,095 days [am = about 1,095 days]. This extended longevity is coupled with a slow, steady growth rate that allows the individual to achieve the remarkable final mantle lengths and body masses documented in trawl surveys. The gonadosomatic index was 15% [GSI = 15%] under those same conditions at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. The delayed attainment of a large body size prior to substantial reproductive investment is a life history strategy consistent with the predictions of bet-hedging theory in stable, low-mortality environments, where the benefits of large size at first reproduction offset the costs of delayed maturity.

Despite the large adult size, the initial starting point for each new generation is exceptionally modest. The mantle length at birth has been confirmed at 1.3 cm [Lb = 1.3 cm], a figure that represents an enormous relative increase over the life of the animal, with females growing from this tiny hatchling size to a mantle length at death that can exceed 270 cm [Li = 270 cm]. The precise upper range of this parameter extends to 275 cm (265-275 cm) [Li = 265-275 cm] based on the largest verified specimens, indicating that while 270 cm is a representative value, some individuals may reach or slightly exceed this boundary. The corresponding body mass at that terminal size is extraordinary, with the estimated wet weight at death being 198,000 grams [Wwi = 198,000 grams]. This immense weight, distributed across the elongated, conical mantle, represents a significant biomass contribution to the deep-sea community and likely influences local predator-prey dynamics wherever the species is abundant.

The timing of major life history events is tightly coupled to the thermal regime of the squid's environment, with the majority of available data derived from specimens and experiments conducted at a stable temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. The mantle length at puberty was 100 cm [Lp = 100 cm], and the gonadosomatic index reached a maximum of 15% [GSI = 15%] at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. The sheer scale of the species is perhaps best appreciated by considering the growth multiple from birth to death; a neonate with a mantle length of just 1.3 cm [Lb = 1.3 cm] will, over the course of its life, achieve a final length of approximately 270 cm [Li = approximately 270 cm] and a wet weight on the order of 198,000 grams [Wwi = 198,000 grams], exemplifying one of the most dramatic ontogenetic size increases among the pelagic squids.
